p.src: As master and disciple stood looking, a crash suddenly sounded from the middle of the stream. A dragon burst forth, driving the waves before it, sprang above the rocky bank, and lunged at the elder. In alarm, the Pilgrim dropped the luggage, swept his master down from the horse, and fled back with him. Unable to catch them, the dragon swallowed the white horse, saddle and bridle together, in a single gulp, then submerged once more and vanished beneath the water. The Pilgrim seated his master on high ground, then returned to fetch the horse and shoulder the baggage. He found only the single load of luggage; the horse was gone. He carried the luggage back to his master and said, “Master, that accursed dragon has vanished. It has frightened my horse away, though.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, how are we to find the horse?” The Pilgrim replied, “Do not worry. Wait here while I go and look.”

p.src: He gave a whistle and leapt into the air. Shading his fiery, golden-pupiled eyes with one hand, he surveyed every direction, but could find no trace of the horse. Descending from the clouds, he reported, “Master, our horse was certainly eaten by that dragon. I have searched all around, and it is nowhere to be seen.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, how could that creature have a mouth large enough to eat such a great horse, saddle and bridle included? It must have panicked, slipped its reins, and run into some hollow in the mountains. Look again, more carefully.” The Pilgrim said, “You do not know what I am capable of. In broad daylight, these eyes of mine can ordinarily discern good or ill a thousand leagues away. If a dragonfly spread its wings anywhere within a thousand leagues, I would see it. How could I fail to see such a great horse?” Tripitaka said, “If it has been eaten, how am I to continue onward? Alas! How can I cross these countless mountains and rivers?” As he spoke, his tears fell like rain. When the Pilgrim saw him begin to weep, his fiery temper could bear it no longer. He shouted, “Master, do not be such a spineless weakling! Sit here, sit here, while Old Monkey finds that wretch and makes him return our horse.” Only then did Tripitaka seize hold of him and say, “Disciple, where will you go to find it? I fear it may leap out secretly and kill me as well. If both man and horse are lost, what shall we do then?” Hearing this, the Pilgrim grew still angrier and roared like thunder, “You are utterly hopeless, hopeless! You want a horse to ride, yet you will not let me go after it. If that is how it is, then sit here watching the luggage until you grow old!”

p.src: He was still grumbling and shouting, unable to master his anger, when a voice spoke from the air: “Great Sage Sun, do not be angry; Imperial Brother Tang, cease your weeping. We are the deities stationed along this road by the Bodhisattva Guanyin, sent especially to protect the scripture pilgrim in secret.” Hearing this, the elder hurriedly bowed in reverence. The Pilgrim said, “Who are you all? State your names, so that I may call the roll.” The gods replied, “We are the Six Ding and Six Jia, the Guardians of the Five Regions, the Merit Officers of the Four Watches, and the eighteen monastery guardians who protect the faith. Each of us takes a turn on duty, awaiting orders.” The Pilgrim asked, “Whose turn begins today?” The Guardians replied, “The Ding and Jia, the Merit Officers, and the monastery guardians serve by turns. Of us Guardians of the Five Regions, however, the Golden-Headed Guardian alone remains constantly at your side, day and night.” The Pilgrim said, “In that case, those not on duty may withdraw. Let the Six Ding divine generals, the Merit Officer on duty today, and all the Guardians remain here to protect my master. Old Monkey will seek out that accursed dragon in the stream and make it return my horse.” The gods obeyed his command. Only then did Tripitaka set his mind at ease. Sitting upon a rocky ledge, he cautioned the Pilgrim to take care. The Pilgrim said, “Set your mind entirely at ease.” Good Monkey King! He tightened his cotton robe, hitched up his tiger-skin kilt, gripped his gold-banded iron staff, and roused his spirit. Going straight to the ravine, half veiled in cloud and mist, he hovered above the water and shouted, “You wretched mud-eel, give me back my horse! Give me back my horse!”

p.src: Back and forth they fought for a long while, circling for many rounds. At last the dragon’s strength failed and its sinews grew numb. Unable to withstand its opponent, it wheeled around, plunged into the water again, and hid deep at the bottom of the stream, refusing to show its head. Though the Monkey King cursed it without cease, it merely pretended to be deaf.

p.src: With nothing more he could do, the Pilgrim returned to Tripitaka and said, “Master, Old Monkey’s curses drew the monster out. It fought me for a long while, but then lost its nerve and fled. Now it is hiding in the water and refuses to come out again.” Tripitaka said, “But are you certain it was truly the creature that ate my horse?” The Pilgrim replied, “Just listen to yourself! If it had not eaten the horse, would it have answered my challenge and come out to oppose Old Monkey?” Tripitaka said, “The other day, when you killed the tiger, you said you possessed the arts to subdue dragons and tame tigers. Why can you not subdue this one today?” Now the monkey could never endure being goaded by others. At this rebuke from Tripitaka, he summoned his divine might and said, “Say no more, say no more! I shall go and settle once and for all which of us is stronger.”

p.src: The Monkey King strode away and leapt to the stream bank. Exercising his power to overturn rivers and churn the seas, he stirred the crystal-clear waters of the steep Eagle Grief Stream into waves like the Yellow River flooding through its nine bends. Deep in the ravine, the accursed dragon could neither sit nor lie at ease. It thought to itself, “Good fortune never comes in pairs, while misfortune never comes alone. I only just escaped a death sentence under the laws of Heaven, and before even a year has passed while I live here as circumstances allow, I have encountered this vicious fiend, who has come to harm me.” The more it thought, the angrier it became. Unable to endure the humiliation, it clenched its teeth, leapt out, and cursed, “Where did you come from, you vicious fiend, to bully me so?” The Pilgrim replied, “Never mind where I come from. Just return the horse, and I shall spare your life.” The dragon said, “I swallowed your horse into my belly. How could I possibly spit it out again? I will not return it. What are you going to do about it?” The Pilgrim said, “If you will not return the horse, then taste my staff! I shall beat you to death and take your life in payment for my horse’s.” The two fought bitterly once more beneath the mountain cliff. After only a few rounds, the young dragon truly could not withstand him. With a shake of its body, it transformed into a little water snake and slipped away into the grass.

p.src: The Monkey King, cudgel in hand, hurried forward, parting the grass in search of the snake, but could find no trace of it. So furious was he that his Three Corpse Spirits raged and smoke poured from his seven orifices. He uttered the spell “Om,” summoning the local God of the Soil and the mountain god, who came together, knelt, and announced, “The mountain god and the God of the Soil present themselves.” The Pilgrim said, “Stick out your shins. Five strokes apiece by way of greeting will help old Sun vent his spleen.” The two gods knocked their heads upon the ground and pleaded, “We beg the Great Sage to show mercy and allow these humble gods to explain.” The Pilgrim said, “What have you to say?” The two gods said, “The Great Sage was imprisoned for so long that we did not know when you had emerged, and so failed to welcome you. We humbly beg forgiveness.” The Pilgrim said, “In that case, I shall spare you the beating for now. But tell me: where did that monstrous dragon in Eagle Grief Stream come from? Why did he seize and devour my master’s white horse?” The two gods said, “The Great Sage has never had a master. You were originally a primordial immortal who submitted to neither Heaven nor Earth. How could there be any such thing as your master’s horse?” The Pilgrim said, “You know nothing about it. It was solely because of that business of deceiving my superiors that I suffered these five hundred years of torment. Now, through the Bodhisattva Guanyin’s exhortation to goodness, a true monk from the Tang emperor’s realm was sent to free me and take me as his disciple, so that I might follow him to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. As we passed this place, my master’s white horse was lost.” The two gods said, “So that is how matters stand. There has never been anything evil in this stream. It is merely deep, precipitous, and broad, with water so limpid that its light reaches the bottom; even crows and magpies dare not fly across it. Seeing their own reflections in the clear water, they mistake them for birds of their own kind and often plunge into the stream. Hence it is called the Steep Stream of Eagle Grief. Only some years ago, when the Bodhisattva Guanyin went in search of the scripture pilgrim, she rescued a jade dragon and placed him here, ordering him to await the pilgrim and forbidding him to commit evil. When hungry, he merely comes ashore to pounce upon birds and magpies, or catches river deer and deer for food. We do not know how he could have been so witless as to offend the Great Sage today.” The Pilgrim said, “The first time, he even crossed weapons with old Sun and circled about for several bouts. The second time, old Sun shouted abuse at him, but he would not come out again. So I used a spell to overturn rivers and churn seas, muddying the waters of his stream. Then he sprang up and tried to contend with me once more. He did not know how heavy old Sun’s cudgel was; unable to ward it off, he changed into a water snake and burrowed into the grass. I chased after him, but found no trace.” The God of the Soil said, “There is something the Great Sage does not know. Ten thousand hollows and channels connect beneath this stream, which is why its waters run so deep and far. There must be an opening here as well, through which he slipped down. The Great Sage need not grow angry and search here. To subdue this creature, you need only invite Guanyin here, and he will naturally submit.”

p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim summoned the mountain god and the God of the Soil, brought them with him to see Tripitaka, and related the entire affair. Tripitaka said, “If you must go and invite the Bodhisattva, when will you ever return? How is this poor monk to endure hunger and cold?” Before he had finished speaking, they heard the Golden-Headed Guardian call from the unseen sky, “Great Sage, you need not stir. This humble god will go and invite the Bodhisattva.” The Pilgrim was delighted and said, “Much obliged, much obliged. Hurry, hurry!” The Guardian swiftly mounted his cloud and went straight to the Southern Sea. The Pilgrim ordered the mountain god and the God of the Soil to guard his master and the Duty God of the Day to seek vegetarian provisions, while he himself returned to patrol the stream. Of this we shall say no more.

p.src: Now the Golden-Headed Guardian mounted his cloud and soon reached the Southern Sea. Lowering his auspicious radiance, he went straight into the Purple Bamboo Grove on Mount Potalaka. Through the golden-armored deities and Moksha Hui’an, he sent word of his arrival and was admitted to the Bodhisattva’s presence. The Bodhisattva asked, “What brings you here?” The Guardian replied, “The Tang Monk lost his horse at the Steep Stream of Eagle Grief on Coiled Snake Mountain, leaving the Great Sage Sun in a desperate quandary. When he questioned the local earth gods, they said it had been swallowed by the accursed dragon whom the Bodhisattva placed in the stream. The Great Sage sent this humble god to ask the Bodhisattva to subdue that accursed dragon and restore his horse.” On hearing this, the Bodhisattva said, “That wretch was originally a son of Ao Run, Dragon King of the Western Sea. He set fire to and burned a bright pearl in the palace, and his father accused him of unfilial rebellion, for which the Heavenly Court condemned him to death. I personally petitioned the Jade Emperor and obtained his release, intending him to serve as a mount for the Tang Monk. How could he instead have eaten the Tang Monk’s horse? If that is what happened, wait here while I go.” The Bodhisattva descended from her lotus throne, left the immortal cave directly, and rode auspicious radiance with the Guardian across the Southern Sea. p.src: Before long, the Bodhisattva and the Guardian reached Coiled Snake Mountain. They halted their auspicious cloud in midair and looked down, where they saw the Pilgrim Sun shouting abuse beside the stream. The Bodhisattva told the Guardian to summon him. The Guardian lowered his cloud and, without passing by Tripitaka, went straight to the stream and told the Pilgrim, “The Bodhisattva has arrived.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim leaped upon his cloud and sprang into the air. He shouted at her, “You teacher of the Seven Buddhas, you merciful leader of the faith—how could you devise a scheme to harm me?” The Bodhisattva said, “You audacious stable ape, you boorish red-bottomed monkey! Again and again I did my utmost to bring a scripture pilgrim here and charged him to save your life. Yet instead of thanking me for the grace that kept you alive, why do you come and raise a clamor against me?” The Pilgrim said, “A fine thing you have done to me! Since you released me, you should simply have let me roam free and enjoy myself. When you met me over the sea the other day, you rebuked me and told me to come serve the Tang Monk with all my heart and strength. That would have been enough. Why did you give him a flowered cap and trick me into wearing it on my head to suffer? You made this band grow fast upon old Sun’s head, then taught him some so-called Tight-Fillet Spell, so that the old monk chants it again and again and makes my head ache again and again. Is that not you harming me?” The Bodhisattva laughed and said, “You monkey! You obey no instruction and will not accept the true fruit. If I did not restrain you in this way, you would again deceive your superiors and defy Heaven, knowing neither good nor evil. If you caused trouble as you did before, who would be able to control you? Only with this fiend upon your head will you consent to enter the path of my Yoga teaching.” The Pilgrim said, “As for that matter, let us suppose it is indeed my personal bane. But why did you also place that guilty, accursed dragon here to become a monster and have him eat my master’s horse? That is letting an evildoer loose to commit wickedness—most uncharitable indeed.” The Bodhisattva said, “That dragon was obtained for this place through my personal petition to the Jade Emperor, expressly to serve as a mount for the scripture pilgrim. Consider: how could an ordinary horse from the Eastern Land cross these myriad rivers and mountains? How could it ever reach the Buddha’s sacred land on Spirit Mountain? Only with this dragon horse can you complete the journey.” The Pilgrim said, “But he is so frightened of old Sun that he hides away and refuses to emerge. What are we to do?” The Bodhisattva called to the Guardian, “Go to the stream and shout, ‘Third Prince Jade Dragon, son of Dragon King Ao Run, come out! The Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea is here.’ Then he will come out.”

u.src: Before long, the Bodhisattva and the Guardian reached Coiled Snake Mountain. They halted their auspicious cloud in midair and looked down, where they saw the Pilgrim Sun shouting abuse beside the stream.
The Bodhisattva told the Guardian to summon him.
The Guardian lowered his cloud and, without passing by Tripitaka, went straight to the stream and told the Pilgrim, “The Bodhisattva has arrived.”

Hearing this, the Pilgrim leaped upon his cloud and sprang into the air. He shouted at her, “You teacher of the Seven Buddhas, you merciful leader of the faith—how could you devise a scheme to harm me?”
The Bodhisattva said, “You audacious stable ape, you boorish red-bottomed monkey!

Again and again I did my utmost to bring a scripture pilgrim here and charged him to save your life. Yet instead of thanking me for the grace that kept you alive, why do you come and raise a clamor against me?”
The Pilgrim said, “A fine thing you have done to me!
Since you released me, you should simply have let me roam free and enjoy myself.

When you met me over the sea the other day, you rebuked me and told me to come serve the Tang Monk with all my heart and strength. That would have been enough. Why did you give him a flowered cap and trick me into wearing it on my head to suffer?

You made this band grow fast upon old Sun’s head, then taught him some so-called Tight-Fillet Spell, so that the old monk chants it again and again and makes my head ache again and again. Is that not you harming me?”

The Bodhisattva laughed and said, “You monkey! You obey no instruction and will not accept the true fruit. If I did not restrain you in this way, you would again deceive your superiors and defy Heaven, knowing neither good nor evil.
If you caused trouble as you did before, who would be able to control you?
Only with this fiend upon your head will you consent to enter the path of my Yoga teaching.”
The Pilgrim said, “As for that matter, let us suppose it is indeed my personal bane.
But why did you also place that guilty, accursed dragon here to become a monster and have him eat my master’s horse?
That is letting an evildoer loose to commit wickedness—most uncharitable indeed.”
The Bodhisattva said, “That dragon was obtained for this place through my personal petition to the Jade Emperor, expressly to serve as a mount for the scripture pilgrim.
Consider: how could an ordinary horse from the Eastern Land cross these myriad rivers and mountains?
How could it ever reach the Buddha’s sacred land on Spirit Mountain?
Only with this dragon horse can you complete the journey.”
The Pilgrim said, “But he is so frightened of old Sun that he hides away and refuses to emerge. What are we to do?”

u.src: The Bodhisattva called to the Guardian, “Go to the stream and shout, ‘Third Prince Jade Dragon, son of Dragon King Ao Run, come out! The Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea is here.’
Then he will come out.”

p.src: The Guardian duly went to the stream and called twice. The young dragon churned the waves and leapt from the water. Taking human form, he mounted a cloud and rose into the air, where he bowed to the Bodhisattva and said, “I once received from you the grace of deliverance and the gift of life. I have waited here a long while, yet have heard no news of the scripture pilgrim.” The Bodhisattva pointed at the Pilgrim and said, “Is this not the scripture pilgrim’s senior disciple?” When the young dragon saw him, he said, “Bodhisattva, this is my enemy. Yesterday I was hungry, and it is true that I ate his horse. Relying on his strength, he fought me until I lost heart and retreated, then cursed me so fiercely that I shut myself in and dared not come out. Yet he never once mentioned the words ‘fetching the scriptures.’” The Pilgrim said, “You never asked my name or surname. How was I supposed to tell you?” The young dragon said, “Did I not ask what place a vicious fiend like you had come from? You shouted, ‘What does it matter where I am from? Just give me back my horse!’ When did you ever utter so much as half the word ‘Tang’?” The Bodhisattva said, “That monkey relies entirely on his own prowess. How could he ever bring himself to commend another? As you journey onward, however, there will be others destined to submit and join you. Whenever you question someone, first mention the fetching of the scriptures. Then you will need no effort, for they will naturally bow and submit.”

p.src: The Pilgrim gladly accepted her instruction. The Bodhisattva stepped forward and removed the bright pearl beneath the young dragon’s neck. Dipping her willow sprig into sweet dew, she brushed his body with it, breathed out a breath of immortal air, and cried, “Transform!” At once the dragon assumed the exact coat and appearance of the original horse. She further instructed him, saying, “You must devote yourself to discharging your karmic debt. When your merit is complete, you shall rise above the common dragons, and I shall grant you a golden body and the true fruit of enlightenment.” With the bit held between his teeth, the young dragon understood and inwardly gave his assent. The Bodhisattva told Wukong to lead him back to meet Tripitaka. “I shall return to the ocean.” The Pilgrim seized hold of the Bodhisattva and refused to let go, saying, “I will go no farther! I will go no farther! The road to the West is so rough and perilous. How long will it take me to protect this mortal monk all the way there? With so many trials and tribulations, even old Monkey can scarcely preserve his life. How could I ever achieve any merit or reward? I will go no farther! I will go no farther!” The Bodhisattva said, “In former days, before you had attained the human path, you were willing to devote yourself wholeheartedly to cultivation and awakening; now that you have escaped the calamities of Heaven, why have you instead grown indolent? Our school attains truth through quiescent extinction; you must have faith in attaining the true fruit. If you should reach a place of bitter trial where your body is imperilled, I promise that when you call upon Heaven, Heaven shall answer, and when you call upon Earth, Earth shall respond. And if you truly come to a crisis from which there is no escape, I shall personally come to save you. Come here, and I shall bestow one more skill upon you.” The Bodhisattva plucked three leaves from her willow sprig, placed them behind the Pilgrim’s head, and cried, “Transform!” They instantly became three life-saving hairs. She instructed him, “When you find yourself helpless and without support, you may transform them as circumstances require and thereby save yourself from urgent suffering and disaster.” Only after hearing all these kindly words did the Pilgrim thank the greatly merciful and compassionate Bodhisattva. Encircled by fragrant breezes and drifting rainbow mists, the Bodhisattva went straight back to Mount Putuo.

p.src: Only then did the Pilgrim lower his cloud. Gripping the dragon-horse by its forelock, he brought it before Tripitaka and said, “Master, we have a horse now.” Tripitaka was delighted at the sight and said, “Disciple, why does this horse look rather fatter and sturdier than the old one? Where did you find it?” The Pilgrim said, “Master, you are still dreaming. Just now the Golden-Headed Guardian invited the Bodhisattva here, and she transformed the dragon in the stream into our white horse. Its coat and appearance are the same; only the saddle and bridle are missing. She told old Monkey to drag it back here.” Greatly startled, Tripitaka said, “Where is the Bodhisattva? Let me go and bow to her in thanks.” The Pilgrim said, “By now the Bodhisattva has already reached the Southern Sea. She had no patience to linger.” Tripitaka gathered earth into an altar, burned incense, and bowed toward the south. When he had finished bowing, he rose and prepared to continue onward with the Pilgrim. The Pilgrim dismissed the mountain and local gods, gave instructions to the Guardian and the Merit Officer, and then asked his master to mount. Tripitaka said, “How can I ride a horse without saddle or bridle? Let us first find a boat to cross the stream, and then decide what to do.” The Pilgrim said, “Master, you truly have no sense of present circumstances! Where would a boat come from in these wild mountains? This horse has lived here for a long time and must know the currents. Just ride him across as though he were a boat.”

p.src: Tripitaka had no alternative and could only follow his advice, mounting the bareback horse. The Pilgrim shouldered the luggage. They reached the edge of the stream. Upstream they saw an old fisherman poling a raft of deadwood down with the current. Seeing him, the Pilgrim beckoned and called, “Old fisherman, come here! Come here! We are journeying from the Eastern Land to fetch the scriptures. My master cannot cross here, so come and ferry him over.” Hearing this, the fisherman hurriedly poled over to them. The Pilgrim asked his master to dismount and supported him at his side. Tripitaka boarded the raft; they hauled the horse aboard and secured the luggage. The old fisherman pushed off, and the raft sped like the wind and flew like an arrow. Before they knew it, they had crossed the Eagle-Grief Torrent and landed on the western bank. Tripitaka told the Pilgrim to open the bundle and take out a few coins of Great Tang currency to give the old fisherman. With one thrust of his pole, the old fisherman sent the raft away, saying, “I want no money! I want no money!” He vanished into the vast and misty midstream. Tripitaka felt deeply obliged and kept pressing his palms together in thanks. The Pilgrim said, “Master, do not trouble yourself over it. Did you not recognize him? He is the water god of this stream. Because he failed to come and receive old Monkey, I ought properly to give him a beating. Merely sparing him a beating is reward enough. How would he dare ask for money?” The master half believed him and half did not. He could only mount the bareback horse once more and follow the Pilgrim onto the highroad, heading straight west. Indeed: Vast True Suchness mounts the farther shore; with sincere heart, one perfects one’s nature and ascends Vulture Peak.

p.src: From horseback, Tripitaka gazed into the distance and suddenly saw a manor beside the road. Tripitaka said, “Wukong, there is a household ahead where we can ask for lodging. We shall continue tomorrow morning.” The Pilgrim raised his head, looked, and said, “Master, that is no family manor.” Tripitaka said, “How is it not?” The Pilgrim said, “A family manor would not have roof ridges adorned with flying fish and crouching beasts. That is certainly a temple or convent.”

p.src: As master and disciple talked, they soon arrived at the gate. Tripitaka dismounted and saw three large characters over the gate: “Village Shrine.” He then went inside. Inside was an old man with prayer beads around his neck. He came forward with palms joined and said, “Master, please be seated.” Tripitaka hurriedly returned the courtesy, then entered the hall and bowed before the sacred image. The old man at once called a boy to serve tea. When the tea was finished, Tripitaka asked the old man, “Why is this temple called a ‘Village Shrine’?” The old man replied, “This humble place lies within the borders of the Western Tibetan kingdom of Hami. Behind this temple is a village whose households joined in sincere devotion to build this sanctuary. ‘Village’ means the land of a local community; and ‘shrine’ refers to the earth god of that community. Whenever the time comes for spring ploughing, summer weeding, autumn harvesting, or winter storage, every household prepares the three sacrificial animals, flowers, and fruit and comes here to worship the earth god, praying that all four seasons may be peaceful and auspicious, the five grains abundant, and the six kinds of livestock flourishing.” Hearing this, Tripitaka nodded in admiration. “Just as the saying goes, ‘Three miles from home, and the customs are those of another country.’ Where I come from, people have no such worthy custom.” The old man then asked, “And where is your blessed homeland, Master?” Tripitaka replied, “This poor monk comes from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land. By imperial command, I am journeying to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. Passing by your venerable sanctuary as evening draws near, I have come especially to this holy shrine to ask for one night’s lodging. At daybreak I shall depart.” The old man was delighted. After apologizing several times for not having welcomed them properly, he called the boy to prepare a meal. When Tripitaka had eaten, he offered his thanks.

p.src: Sharp-eyed Pilgrim noticed a clothesline beneath the eaves. He went over, tore it down with one tug, and used it to tether the horse by the leg. The old man laughed. “Where did you steal that horse?” Pilgrim snapped angrily, “You old fellow, you have no sense of how to speak to your betters. We are holy monks going to worship the Buddha. Would we steal a horse?” The old man laughed. “If it was not stolen, why does it have neither saddle, bridle, nor reins, so that you must tear down my clothesline?” Tripitaka apologized, saying, “This mischievous fellow is merely hot-tempered. —If you wanted to tether the horse, you should have politely asked the old gentleman for a rope. Why did you tear down his clothesline? —Good sir, please do not take offense. Please forgive him. To tell you the truth, this horse of mine was not stolen. Yesterday, as we came from the east and reached the steep stream of Eagle Grief, I still had the white horse I had originally ridden, complete with saddle and bridle. Unexpectedly, a wicked dragon in the stream had become a monster, and it swallowed my horse, saddle, bridle, and all, in a single gulp. Fortunately, my disciple possesses some ability, and his efforts moved the Bodhisattva Guanyin to come to the stream and subdue the dragon. She made it transform into a white horse exactly like my former mount, hair and hide alike, to carry me westward to worship the Buddha. It has not yet been a full day since we crossed the stream and came to your holy shrine, so we have had no chance to obtain a saddle or bridle.” The old man said, “Master, please do not take offense. I was only making a joke; how was I to know your worthy disciple would take it seriously? When I was young, I too had a little village wealth and delighted in riding a fine horse. But after years of misfortune, bereavement, and fire, I was left with nothing in the end. So I became the keeper of this shrine and now tend its incense and offerings. Fortunately, I live on alms from the benefactors in the village behind the shrine. I still have a saddle and bridle that I have always treasured. Even in such poverty, I could never bring myself to sell them. But now I have heard you say that even the Bodhisattva showed compassion to the divine dragon and made it into a horse to carry you. Surely this old man cannot fail to offer some small assistance. Tomorrow I shall fetch that saddle and bridle and present them to you, good Master. Put them on the horse and continue your journey; I beg you to accept this humble gift.” At these words, Tripitaka thanked him profusely. Soon the boy appeared with their evening vegetarian meal. After they had eaten, lamps were lit and bedding laid out, and each of them retired for the night.

Ask him for them, and do not let him off.” Before he had finished speaking, the old man appeared, carrying a saddle and bridle, saddle padding, reins, halter, and every other item needed for a horse. p.src: Pilgrim was secretly delighted. He fitted the saddle and bridle to the horse, and they suited it as though they had been made to measure. Tripitaka bowed in thanks to the old man, who hurriedly helped him up and said, “You embarrass me, you embarrass me. Why trouble yourself to thank me?” The old man did not detain them further but invited Tripitaka to mount. The elder came out through the gate, grasped the saddle, and mounted. Pilgrim shouldered the luggage. The old man then drew a whip from his sleeve. It had a fragrant rattan handle studded inch by inch with leather knobs and a lash braided from tiger sinew and silk. Standing by the roadside, he offered it with joined hands and said, “Holy Monk, I have one more thing to hold in your hand. Let me give this to you as well.” Tripitaka accepted it from horseback, saying, “Many thanks for your charity, many thanks indeed.”

p.src: Just as he was making a respectful salutation, the old man suddenly vanished. When they turned to look at the Village Shrine, there was nothing but an empty patch of ground. Then they heard a voice speaking from midair: “Holy Monk, forgive our poor hospitality. We are the mountain god and earth god of Mount Potalaka. The Bodhisattva sent us to deliver the saddle and bridle to you. Strive onward to the west, and do not grow negligent even for a moment.” Startled, Tripitaka tumbled from the saddle, bowed toward the sky, and said, “This disciple is but a mortal of flesh and his eyes are blind to divine things. I failed to recognize your venerable forms; I beg forgiveness. Please convey to the Bodhisattva my profound gratitude for her gracious protection.” Just look at him kowtowing endlessly toward the heavens, without even counting how many times. At the roadside the Great Sage Sun nearly collapsed with laughter, while the Handsome Monkey King was beside himself with glee. He stepped forward, pulled at the Tang Monk, and said, “Master, get up. p.src: For the next two months they travelled in peace, encountering only Luoluo tribesmen, Muslims, wolves, tigers, and leopards. Time passed swiftly, and once more it was early spring. The mountains and forests were clothed in brocade green, and the plants and grasses put forth tender shoots; the last plum blossoms had fallen, and the first willow buds were opening. Master and disciple journeyed on, enjoying the spring scenery, until once again they saw the sun sinking in the west. Tripitaka reined in his horse and gazed into the distance. In a hollow among the hills, the dim shapes of towers rose, with shadowy halls and pavilions beyond. Tripitaka said, “Wukong, look. What sort of place is that?” Pilgrim looked up and replied, “If those are not palace halls, then they must belong to a monastery. Let us make haste and ask for lodging there.” Tripitaka gladly agreed, gave the dragon horse its head, and rode straight toward the place.
